 Prolonged haze threatens fruit and vegetable yields in Malaysia
 Prolonged haze in Malaysia could affect fruit and vegetable cultivation by reducing sunlight, potentially leading to lower yields, tighter supplies, and higher consumer prices.
 Vegetable Farmers Association president Lim Ser Kwee said smoke particles reduce sunlight availability, disrupting photosynthesis and slowing crop development. Leafy vegetables, including choy sum, spinach, lettuce, and mustard greens, are particularly vulnerable, while tomatoes, chillies, and cucumbers could experience disruptions during flowering and fruit development.
 The extent of crop losses would depend on haze duration, severity, crop varieties, and weather conditions. Reduced domestic harvests could increase reliance on imports, although transportation costs, exchange rates, and supply disruptions could affect prices.
 Fruit Farmers Association secretary-general Melvin Long said reduced sunlight could affect carbohydrate accumulation, fruit size, maturity, and yields. Passion fruit, guava, papaya, and watermelon are among the crops potentially affected.
 According to Malaysia's Department of Statistics, the country's self-sufficiency ratio reached 132.3 per cent for papaya and 124.9 per cent for watermelon in 2025.
 Both associations called for measures to support growers, including technical assistance, irrigation infrastructure, protected cultivation systems, and financial support where crop losses occur.
